CA Cancer J Clin . 2026 ; e70045 . doi: 10.3322/caac.70045 41400551 INTRODUCTION The American Cancer Society (ACS) first reported on cancer disparities by race and income in the United States in 1986, 1 , 2 followed by numerous publications in the following years. 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 The American Cancer Society’s Report on the Status of Cancer Disparities in the United States , started in 2021, is a biennial publication to examine disparities in cancer occurrence and outcomes and contributing factors to these disparities in the United States by sex, race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status (SES), and geographic location. 10 , 11 This report also provides information on ACS programs targeting cancer disparities and policy recommendations. MATERIALS AND METHODS Data sources Cancer occurrence Data on cancer incidence and stage at diagnosis from 2018 through 2022 by race and ethnicity were obtained from the North American Association of Central Cancer Registries (NAACCR) 12 and by urbanicity of county of residence from the National Cancer Institute’s (NCI’s) Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) 21 registry program. 13 Data on cancer survival in patients with cancer aged 99 years and younger diagnosed in 2016 through 2022 were obtained from the SEER 21 cancer registries (excluding Illinois) 13 and on cancer mortality in 2019 through 2023 from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC’s) National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). 14 All cancer occurrence data were stratified by age group, sex, race, ethnicity, urbanicity of the county of residence, and cancer type. The latter included all cancers combined and four leading causes of cancer death in each sex, i.e., cancers of the lung and bronchus (lung), female breast (breast), prostate, colorectum, and pancreas, all of which except pancreatic cancer are recommended for screening in average‐risk populations, as well as uterine cervix (cervical) cancer—the other screenable cancer. Data on colorectal cancer incidence, stage at diagnosis, and survival excluded cancer of the appendix. Consistent with our previous report, we stratified the analysis into two age groups: younger than 65 years and 65 years and older. This cutoff reflects the near universal eligibility for Medicare coverage at age 65 years and the finding that disparities in cancer occurrence are more pronounced among individuals younger than 65 years compared with older adults. 11 Self‐identified race and ethnicity categories included non‐Hispanic White (White), non‐Hispanic Black (Black), non‐Hispanic American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN), non‐Hispanic Asian and Pacific Islander (API), and Hispanic‐Latinx (Hispanic) populations. It should be noted that race and ethnicity are sociopolitical constructs and do not delineate distinct biologic categories. 15 Cancer incidence, stage at diagnosis, and survival data for the AIAN population were confined to individuals residing in Purchased/Referred Care Delivery Area counties, which cover approximately two thirds of the AIAN population, to minimize racial misclassification. 7 , 16 Mortality rates for the AIAN population (for the entire United States) were adjusted for racial misclassification on death certificates using classification ratios previously published by the NCHS. 17 Urbanicity was defined based on the 2013 Rural‐Urban Continuum Codes, 18 but using three consolidated categories: county of residence in a large metropolitan area (with a population of ≥1 million), a small‐medium metropolitan area (with a population of <1 million), and a nonmetropolitan area. To estimate cancer mortality rates by education level in individuals aged 25–74 years, mortality data for 2019–2023 were obtained from the NCHS by sex, race and ethnicity (all, White, Black), cancer (all‐cancer, lung, colorectum, breast, and prostate), and highest education level attained (≤12, 13‐15, and ≥16 years of education). 19 The corresponding population data based on US census microdata were obtained through IPUMS USA. 20 For records with missing information on education attainment and race and ethnicity (approximately 1.5% and 0.2% of mortality data, respectively), values were imputed according to the overall distribution of available categories within each variable. To estimate sex‐specific and cancer‐specific cancer mortality rates in 2019–2023 by congressional district, we constructed cancer mortality and population data for 436 congressional districts corresponding to the 435 seats of the US House of Representatives among the 50 states plus the District of Columbia, which elects a nonvoting delegate to the House. District boundaries were defined according to the 119th Congress of the United States, in effect from January 2025 to January 2027. 21 We used state‐level data for seven congressional districts that comprised an entire state (Alaska, Delaware, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont, and Wyoming) or followed federal district boundaries (District of Columbia). Some other congressional districts comprise an entire county or a group of counties. For districts that encompassed part of one or several counties, we first estimated the sex‐specific population within each census block within the district using the 2020 US Census data. Then, the number of cancer deaths and the population from the NCHS in each county were weighted by the sex‐specific proportion of the block population to estimate the number of cancer deaths and population in the block. 22 The number of cancer deaths and population were aggregated over the blocks and counties that were included in the given congressional district. Socioeconomic status and social determinants of health Data on educational attainment of ≤12 years, income below the federal poverty level (FPL), delay or nonreceipt of medical care because of cost, measures of housing insecurity (inability to pay mortgage, rent, or utility bills) and food insecurity (inability to afford balanced meals), and health insurance coverage were obtained from self‐reported measures in the 2024 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). 23 Health insurance coverage was categorized into uninsured, Medicaid or other public only, and private for individuals younger than 65 years; and Medicare only (including Medicare Advantage), Medicare plus public only (Medicare dually eligible), and Medicare plus private (Medicare supplemental) for individuals aged 65 years and older. More information on insurance categories is available in the Supporting Methods. Cancer risk factors and screening Data on prevalence of ever and current cigarette smoking, obesity, heavy alcohol drinking, and physical inactivity in 2024 by age group, sex, race, ethnicity, and urbanicity of the county of residence in individuals aged 18 years and older were obtained from self‐reported measures in the NHIS. 23 Ever cigarette smoking was defined as smoking at least 100 cigarettes in a lifetime. Current cigarette smoking was defined as smoking at least 100 cigarettes in a lifetime and currently smoking every day or some days. Obesity was defined as a body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m 2 . The prevalence of obesity in the United States generally is estimated based on BMI values measured on physical examination in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 24 but, because information on urbanicity is not available from this survey, we report obesity estimates from the NHIS. Heavy alcohol drinking was defined as greater than 14 drinks per week in the past year for men or greater than seven drinks per week in the past year for women. Alcohol consumption levels are usually adjusted for underreporting using a same adjustment factor for all subpopulations based on alcohol sales data. 25 We defined heavy alcohol consumption based on unadjusted consumption levels only to compare the exposures across categories of race and ethnicity and urbanicity. Physical inactivity was defined as the absence of any aerobic leisure‐time physical activity. Some surveys do not collect data on the same items in every cycle. Data on being up to date with the utilization of screening according to the ACS guidelines and US Preventive Services Task Force recommendations for cancers of the female breast (2023), colorectum (2023), cervix (2021), and prostate (2023) by age group, race, ethnicity, and urbanicity of the county of residence were based on data from the NHIS. 23 We relied on a previous report and method to estimate lung cancer screening rates nationally and by state in 2022 based on the CDC’s Prevention Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data 26 because the NHIS has not collected detailed full‐year lung cancer screening data since 2015. 27 Statistical methods Age‐standardized incidence and mortality rates per 100,000 population and 5‐year relative survival were calculated using SEER*Stat software, version 9.0.41.4. Incidence and mortality rate ratios (RRs) and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using SEER*Stat software and Stata, version 15.1 (Stata Corporation), based on age‐adjusted rates and Tiwari and colleagues' method. 28 For confidentiality reasons and to produce more stable results, rates were suppressed when there were <16 cancer cases or deaths in each group. 29 Weighted prevalence estimates for measures of SES, social determinants of health (SDOH), risk factors, and cancer screening by corresponding stratifications were calculated using R, version 4.5.1 (R Core Team), and SAS‐callable SUDAAN, release 11.0.4 (SAS Institute Inc.), and accounted for the complex survey designs. To obtain stable results, prevalence estimates were suppressed when a denominator size was <50 or the relative standard error was ≥0.3. 24 DISPARITIES IN CANCER OCCURRENCE Cancer incidence During 2018 through 2022, incidence rates were higher in Black males than in White males for all cancers combined and for each evaluated cancer type (Table  1 ). In addition, incidence rates were higher in Black females than in White females for cancers of the colorectum, pancreas, and cervix (Table  1 ). Incidence rates were also higher in AIAN males for lung and colorectal cancers and in AIAN females for all cancers combined and for lung, colorectal, pancreatic, and cervical cancers than in their White counterparts. In contrast, incidence rates for all cancers combined and for each evaluated cancer type in both sexes were lower in API and Hispanic populations than in the White population, except for a higher cervical cancer rate in Hispanic females relative to White females. Cancer stage at diagnosis Compared with the White population, the proportion of localized‐stage cancers during 2018 through 2022 was lower among all other racial and ethnic groups for cancers of the lung, breast, prostate (except the Black population), colorectum (except the API population), and cervix (Figure  2 ). For pancreatic cancer, however, the proportion of localized‐stage cancers was comparable, and low, across all evaluated racial and ethnic groups, including the White population. Currently, there are no accepted modalities for pancreatic cancer screening in average‐risk populations. Compared with individuals residing in counties in large metropolitan areas, individuals residing in nonmetropolitan areas had lower proportions of localized‐stage lung, breast, pancreatic, and cervical cancers during 2018 through 2022. Differences in the proportion of localized‐stage cancer diagnosis by race and ethnicity and urbanicity were generally similar in those younger than 65 years and aged 65 years and older, with a notable exception of cervical cancer, for which the observed differences were greater in females younger than 65 years (see Figure S1 ); currently, cervical cancer screening is recommended through age 65 years. Cancer survival The 5‐year age‐standardized relative survival during 2016 through 2022 for evaluated cancer types was generally lowest in Black and AIAN populations (Figure  3 ; see Figure S2 ). Similarly, stage‐specific survival was generally lower in Black and AIAN populations than in the White population, e.g., 36% and 30% versus 47%, respectively, for localized‐stage pancreatic cancer (see Table S3 ). When stratified by urbanicity of the county of residence, the age‐standardized 5‐year relative cancer survival for evaluated cancers during 2016 through 2022 was lower in nonmetropolitan areas than in large metropolitan areas, e.g., 59% versus 64% for cervical cancer (Figure  3 ), and for each stage at diagnosis, e.g., 57% versus 71% for localized‐stage lung cancer (see Table S3 ). Cancer mortality The mortality rate for all cancers combined during 2019 through 2023 was higher in Black and AIAN males (by 14% and 13%, respectively) and females (by 10% and 22%, respectively) than in their White counterparts (Table  1 ). The 10% higher cancer mortality in Black females than in White females was despite a 9% lower overall cancer incidence rates in Black females. Mortality rates for each evaluated cancer were higher in Black and AIAN males than in White males, except pancreatic cancer, for which mortality rates were comparable in AIAN and White males. A similar pattern was observed for Black and AIAN females, except for a lower lung cancer mortality rate in Black females than in White females. With the exception of a 14% higher cervical cancer mortality rate among Hispanic females, mortality rates for each evaluated cancer type were lower in API and Hispanic males and females than in their White counterparts. When evaluated by urbanicity of the county of residence, overall cancer mortality rates during 2019 through 2023 were higher in nonmetropolitan areas than in large metropolitan areas by 23% in males and 18% in females, about twice the magnitude of the incidence disparity (Table  2 ). Nonmetropolitan areas also had higher mortality rates for each evaluated cancer type, including breast and prostate cancers, despite lower incidence rates. The largest difference by urbanicity was observed for lung cancer, with mortality rates 47% higher in males and 40% higher in females in nonmetropolitan areas compared with large metropolitan areas; this was followed by cervical cancer (36% higher) and colorectal cancer (28% higher in males and 27% in females). When stratified jointly by urbanicity and race and ethnicity, the Black–White difference in overall cancer mortality rates in females was greater in large metropolitan areas than in nonmetropolitan areas, whereas the difference in males was similar across both settings (see Table S4 ). Cancer mortality rates during 2019 through 2023 were higher among adults with lower SES (Table  3 ). The differences by education were substantially larger than by race, indicating that SES plays a major role in driving racial disparities in cancer mortality. Overall cancer mortality rates were higher in Black adults than in White adults with the same education level by 7%–28% among males and 2%–43% among females. Compared with their counterparts who had ≥16 years of education, however, the rate in adults who had ≤12 years of education was higher by 71% in Black females, by 2.4 times in Black males and White females, and by 2.9 times in White males. For the evaluated cancer types, mortality rates within each educational attainment category were higher in the Black population than in the White population, with the exception of lung cancer in males with ≤12 years of education and females with ≤16 years of education, among whom the rates were lower in the Black population. Similar to all cancers combined, differences in mortality were larger by education than by race for lung and colorectal cancers, whereas differences in prostate cancer mortality were larger by race than by education. Of note, the Black–White disparities in mortality from all evaluated cancers within each educational attainment category were generally largest in the highest educational attainment category. Congressional districts with the highest overall cancer mortality rates in both males and females usually were in the South and East North‐Central division of the Midwest (Figure  4 ). These areas include most states that did not expand Medicaid income eligibility under the Affordable Care Act (ACA) 31 and have historically had less restrictive tobacco‐control policies and high smoking prevalence. 32 A similar pattern existed for lung, female breast, and colorectal cancers. However, Alaska and several districts in the central part of the United States were also among districts with the highest colorectal cancer mortality rates among females. Of note, colorectal cancer mortality rates were also among the highest in several districts along the southern border in Texas, despite having relatively low mortality rates for all cancers combined and for the other evaluated cancer types. Congressional districts with the highest prostate cancer mortality rates were spread across the United States without a clear geographic pattern. When stratified by age group, disparities in cancer mortality rates between Black and AIAN populations versus White populations (see Table S1 ), between nonmetropolitan versus large metropolitan areas (Figure  1 ), between Black and White populations across categories of urbanicity (see Table S3 ), and by congressional district (see Figures  S3 and S4 ) were generally larger in the group younger than 65 years than in the older age group, likely reflecting access to care through Medicare. For example, lung cancer mortality rates among females in nonmetropolitan versus large metropolitan areas were 95% higher in individuals younger than 65 years, but they were 26% higher in individuals aged 65 years and older (Figure  1 ). FACTORS CONTRIBUTING TO CANCER DISPARITIES Social determinants of health Structural SDOH, including social, economic, and political mechanisms, result in a set of socioeconomic positions based on income, education, race, ethnicity, geographic location, and other factors. These positions, in turn, shape intermediary determinants of health, including living and working conditions, housing and food security, access to health care, and behavioral and psychosocial factors. 33 , 34 As such, inequalities in SDOH are major drivers for disparities in exposure to risk factors and receipt of preventive care, early detection (including screening), treatment, and long‐term survivorship care for cancer (Figure  5 ). 34 , 35 For example, redlining was a practice implemented in the 1930s and outlawed in 1968 that withheld financial services (including mortgages) from neighborhoods predominantly inhabited by people of racial and ethnic minoritized and lower SES groups. 36 This practice limited opportunities for homeownership and wealth building in those marginalized communities, notably Black neighborhoods, and contributed to residential separatism, persistent underinvestment, and ongoing inequalities. 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 Of note, the Black–White wealth gap has largely remained unchanged since the 1950s. 40 In 2022, the median wealth of Black households was $44,900: about 15% of the median wealth of White households at $285,000. 41 Redlining and residential separatism have been associated with poorer living conditions, 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 higher exposure to risk factors of cancer, 48 , 49 higher risk of advanced‐stage cancer diagnosis, 36 , 50 , 51 , 52 lower receipt of treatment, 53 and poorer cancer outcomes. 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 , 58 FIGURE 5 Social determinants of health and cancer disparities. Inequalities in SDOH are disproportionately experienced by populations defined by race, ethnicity, SES, and place of residence. In 2024, racial and ethnic minoritized groups and people living in nonmetropolitan areas generally were more likely to have lower educational attainment and to experience poverty and food and housing insecurity (Figure  6 ). For example, the proportion of individuals aged 18–64 years with incomes below the FPL in 2024 was substantially higher in AIAN (21.4%), Black (16.0%), and Hispanic (15.7%) populations than in Asian (8.7%) and White (7.7%) populations and in nonmetropolitan (16.4%) than in large metropolitan (9.1%) areas. Health insurance coverage is a major determinant of access to and receipt of health care services and subsequent cancer outcomes in the United States. 59 , 60 Compared with insured individuals aged 18–64 years, uninsured individuals were more likely to delay or not receive needed medical care because of cost (30.8% vs. 8.3%–9.7% in 2024), or not to be up to date with colorectal (76.5% vs. 35.4%–45.4% in 2023) or female breast (65.2% vs. 26.3%–36.7% in 2023) cancer screening (Figure  7 ). In this age group, the Hispanic population (25.3%) had the highest proportion of individuals with no health insurance in 2024, followed by AIAN (13.3%), Black (10.5%), White (7.8%), and Asian (5.4%) populations (Table  4 ). The proportion of uninsured individuals was also higher in nonmetropolitan areas, in individuals with lower education or income levels, and in the South region. The largest disparity was by education level, with 4.3% of individuals who had ≥16 years of education uninsured compared with 31.8% among those who had <12 years of education. Most individuals aged 65 years and older are age‐eligible for Medicare coverage. As such, the proportion of individuals without health insurance coverage is negligible in this age group, although there are substantial differences in the prevalence of dual coverage (Medicare plus Medicaid or private insurance) across the evaluated populations. For example, the prevalence of Medicare plus private insurance was substantially higher in the White population and in individuals with higher education and income levels than in the other groups. title: Global incidence of lip, oral cavity, and pharyngeal cancers by subsite in 2022.
abstract: Cancers of the lip, oral cavity, and pharynx (LOCP) represent a substantial public health challenge worldwide. Using GLOBOCAN national estimates of incidence, detailed cancer registry data from Cancer Incidence in Five Continents, and population statistics from the United Nations, the authors report the distribution of new cases of LOCP cancers in 185 countries by sex in 2022. Age-standardized incidence rates were calculated. For countries lacking registry data, regional averages from high-quality registries were used to impute subsite-specific estimates. Worldwide, 758,000 people were diagnosed with LOCP cancers in 2022, with oral cavity cancer accounting for approximately 42% of cases, followed by oropharynx (19.3%), nasopharynx (15.9%), hypopharynx (11.4%), salivary gland (7.3%), and lip (4.2%) cancers. Oral cavity cancer was the most frequent LOCP subsite among women in 141 countries and among men in 93 countries, and incidence rates were highest in countries in South-Central Asia. Oropharyngeal cancer was the most frequent LOCP subsite among men in 44 countries and among women in five countries across Europe, Northern America, South America, Australia, and New Zealand. Nasopharyngeal cancer was the most common subsite among men in 39 countries and women in 23 countries, mainly in Northern Africa, Middle Africa, and Eastern and South-Eastern Asia. Rates of hypopharyngeal and salivary gland cancers were low globally, although the incidence burden was greater than that of lip cancer. The authors discuss incidence patterns in relation to disease etiology and the prospects of delivering effective cancer control measures, spanning primary prevention, early detection, cancer treatment, and survivorship.

CA Cancer J Clin . 2026 ; 1 ‐ 13 . doi: 10.3322/caac.70048 INTRODUCTION With cancers of the lip, oral cavity, and pharyngeal (LOCP) comprising approximately one in 25 of all new cancer cases and deaths estimated globally in 2022, the disease represents a substantial and growing public health challenge. 1 The estimated 758,000 new cases and 379,100 deaths in 2022 are predicted to increase across the world's regions as a result of population growth and ageing, particularly in low‐income and middle‐income countries (LMICs), which currently account for more than 80% of all LOCP cancer deaths globally. 2 , 3 LOCP cancers are anatomically complex, encompassing several specific subsites, each with distinct etiological profiles. 3 Notably, cancers of the oral cavity are often associated with tobacco (both smoked and smokeless), alcohol, and areca nut use. 4 Although pharyngeal cancers are only partly driven by these factors, cancers of the oropharynx, including the base of tongue and tonsils, are linked to infection by high‐risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV), specifically HPV16 and HPV18, and nasopharyngeal cancers (NPCs) are linked to Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV) infection. 5 Cancers of the lip are associated with exposure to ultraviolet radiation (UV) and tobacco, with anatomic specificities according to the inner (tobacco) or outer (UV) lip. 6 , 7 , 8 In addition, LOCP cancers are strongly associated with socioeconomic factors 9 and are more commonly diagnosed among men than among women and in older age groups. 3 For example, in 2022, the age‐standardized incidence rate (ASR) of LOCP cancers worldwide increased with age at diagnosis, from less than three cases per 100,000 people younger than 50 years, to 26.9 per 100,000 among people aged 50–69 years, and up to 38.0 per 100,000 cases among people aged 70 years and older. 2 Yet rates reached up to 67.4 per 100,000 among older individuals in regions with high LOCP incidence rates overall, such as Melanesia and South‐Central Asia, and 50.8 per 100,000 in Australia and New Zealand. These underlying determinants and multifactorial etiologies suggest that different factors are driving the magnitude and temporal changes in incidence rates of specific subsites and vary substantially in different populations between and within countries. For example, incidence rates of oral cavity cancer are generally decreasing among men in most world regions yet are increasing among women 7 ; meanwhile, rates of oropharyngeal cancer are steadily increasing in men and women, largely in transitioning countries. 10 This predicted growth in the burden of LOCP cancers, the complexity of the evolving patterns in incidence, and the diverse underlying etiologies make the provision of global estimates by subsite essential for health service reforms and local cancer control planning. Most prior assessments worldwide have grouped cancers together according to major disease classification groupings, obscuring the distinctive epidemiology and risk profiles of subsites. 1 , 11 Therefore, the objective of our current study was to provide a comprehensive assessment of the global burden of LOCP cancers, updating previous estimates with more recent, high‐quality cancer incidence data from population‐based cancer registries (PBCRs) by anatomic subsite. 3 For each of the LOCP cancer subsites, we assess the prospects of health promotion (through primary prevention, achieving a reduction in the underlying risk factors), early detection (mainly by visual oral examination), as well as cancer care and survivorship (including recent treatment breakthroughs) with a view to informing effective global prevention and control of LOCP cancers through the development of policies tailored to local cancer profiles. METHODS Data sources We extracted the national incidence estimates of LOCP cancers in 2022 from the GLOBOCAN national database of the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) in 185 countries hosted on the Global Cancer Observatory platform (Cancer Today). 2 Estimates were available for 185 countries for the following cancer sites according to codes from the International Classification of Disease 10th revision (ICD‐10): lip and oral cavity (C00–C06); salivary glands (C07–C08); and oropharynx, including tonsils (C09–C10), nasopharynx (C11), and hypopharynx (C12–C13). Corresponding population data for 2022 were extracted from the United Nations website. 12 The GLOBOCAN estimates are assembled at the national level using the best available sources of cancer incidence data from PBCRs within a given country, and uncertainties are adjusted based on registry coverage and data quality measures, including the degree of national coverage and the timeliness, completeness, and accuracy of reporting. The sources and hierarchy of methods used in compiling the cancer estimates are described in further detail elsewhere. 13 To compile the estimates, the GLOBOCAN authors also redistributed cases with unspecified codes in national or subnational data to specific three‐digit ICD‐10 categories by year, sex (male, female), and age according to the sex‐specific and age‐specific proportions of cases in each specific category: C14.0 (pharynx, unspecified) to C09–C13 (oropharynx, nasopharynx, and hypopharynx), C14.8 (overlapping lesion of lip, oral cavity, and pharynx) to C00–C13 (lip, oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx, and hypopharynx), and C14.2 (Waldeyer ring). In cases for which the four‐digit categories were not available, cases of C14 (other and ill‐defined sites in the lip, oral cavity, and pharynx) were redistributed across C00–C13. 13 We obtained recorded numbers of new cases for diagnoses from 2003 to 2017 of lip (ICD‐10 C00), base of tongue (C01), and oral cavity (C02–C06) cancers from PBCRs included in volumes X–XII of the IARC's Cancer Incidence in Five Continents (CI5) series as well as data from other PBCRs contributing to the IARC's GLOBOCAN national estimates. 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 The use of data from these PBCRs ensures comparability across countries because of the editorial assessment of each registry's comparability, completeness, and validity before acceptance for inclusion in CI5 volumes. In addition, we incorporated data from subnational registries in seven additional countries in the African Cancer Registry Network ( https://www.afcrn.org/ ) 17 , which provides essential information from sub‐Saharan Africa, without which the region would be represented by only 11 registries from six countries included in CI5 volume XII. The number of cases were provided for males and females separately and by 5‐year age group according to the cancer registry. We aggregated subnational registries within countries to obtain national totals, stratified by two age groups (from birth to 64 years and 65 years and older), to calculate sex‐specific and age‐specific proportions of cases per subsite of the combined group of lip and oral cavity cancers. To reduce random variation, we excluded countries that had less than four cases per subsite per sex and excluded age‐specific summation if there were less than four cases per aggregated age group and instead used the proportions for all ages combined. After applying these inclusion criteria, we included registry data from PBCRs in 87 countries (see Table  S1 ). We then applied the registry data proportions of cancers of the lip, base of tongue, and oral cavity to the corresponding GLOBOCAN estimates of lip and oral cavity cancer to obtain cases per subsite in 2022. For 98 countries in which we did not have corresponding local registry data, we applied average proportions of the subsites from countries that had high‐quality data from subnational or national registries within the same United Nations‐defined geographic world region. 18 The region proportions were calculated by aggregating the national subsite estimates per region calculated in the previous step, were stratified by age (from birth to 64 years and 65 years and older) and sex, then applied to their corresponding GLOBOCAN estimates of lip and oral cavity cancer. Given the shared etiology, we combined cases of cancer of the base of tongue with tonsil and oropharynx cancer to define oropharyngeal cancer (C01, C09–C10). We calculated the proportion of cases of each subsite relative to the total number of cases in the combined group of LOCP cancers as estimated in 2022, as well as corresponding subsite‐specific ASRs per 100,000 person‐years for each site based on the 1966 Segi–Doll World standard population. 19 We present the results of countries aggregated according to 18 United Nations world regions and four World Bank income groups. RESULTS Global burden by subsite Of the estimated 758,000 patients diagnosed with LOCP cancer globally in 2022, 71.9% were men, and 28.1% were women. The most commonly diagnosed subsites were cancers of the oral cavity (317,500 cases), oropharynx (146,500 cases), and nasopharynx (120,400 cases), representing 41.9%, 19.3%, and 15.9% of all LOCP cancers, respectively (Figure  1 ; see Table  S2 ). The remaining subsites were hypopharynx (86,300 cases; 11.4%), salivary glands (55,100 cases; 7.3%), and lip (32,200; 4.2%). FIGURE 1 Proportions of lip, oral cavity, and pharyngeal cancer subsites in 2022 by world region. Three‐digit numbers correspond to codes for each subsite from the International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision. Oral cavity cancer (C02–C06) Most LOCP cancers in South‐Central Asia, Southern Africa, and Melanesia‐Micronesia‐Polynesia were cancers of the oral cavity, contributing 59.8%, 48.8%, and 42.1% of all cases, respectively (Figure  1 ). Of all LOCP cancers, oral cavity cancers contributed 40.0% of cases in Northern Europe, 38.8% in Southern Europe, and 37.5% in South America. The lowest proportions of oral cavity cancer were 23.3% in South‐Eastern Asia and 27.8% in Northern Africa. At the national level, the subsite was the most frequent among women in 141 countries and among men in 93 countries, predominantly in South‐Central Asia, Southern and Western Africa, and Western Asia (Figure  2 ). The number of countries in which oral cavity cancer was more common than oropharyngeal cancer is presented in Figure  S1 . Global ASRs of oral cavity cancer were 2.0 per 100,000 women and 4.6 per 100,000 men (Figure  3 ; see Table  S3 ). The ASRs per 100,000 were highest among women in Papua New Guinea (8.1), Bangladesh (6.4), Pakistan (5.9), and India (4.7) and, among men, were highest in India (13.0), Sri Lanka (12.4), Bangladesh (12.0), Pakistan (11.3), and Papua New Guinea (9.6; Figures  4 and 5 ; see Table  S4 ). The incidence rates were also elevated among men in Southern Africa and Eastern and Southern Europe. The lowest rates were among women in countries in the Caribbean and Central America, Western Asia, and Northern and Western Africa. FIGURE 2 The most common lip, oral cavity, and pharyngeal cancer subsites in 2022 by country among (A) women and (B) men. The numbers of countries represented in each ranking group are included in the legend. FIGURE 3 Age‐standardized incidence rates of lip, oral cavity, and pharyngeal cancer by subsite, by sex and country, in 2022. Lines represent countries (those with the highest rate per subsite are highlighted), and diamonds represent the global average. Three‐digit numbers correspond to codes for each subsite from the International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision. FIGURE 4 Age‐standardized incidence rate of lip, oral cavity, and pharyngeal cancer subsites among women in 2022 by country. Three‐digit numbers correspond to codes for each subsite from the International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision. FIGURE 5 Age‐standardized incidence rate of lip, oral cavity, and pharyngeal cancer subsites among men in 2022 by country. Three‐digit numbers correspond to codes for each subsite from the International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision. Oropharyngeal cancer (C01, C09–C10) The greatest proportion of oropharyngeal cancers was in North America (43.8%) (Figure  1 ), followed by Western and Northern Europe and South America, with somewhat lower proportions between 33.5% and 36.5%. In South‐Eastern Asia, Western Asia, and Northern Africa, less than 10% of all LOCP cancers were cancers of the oropharynx. At the national level, the subsite was the most frequent LOCP cancer among women in five countries (Bolivia, Dominican Republic, Romania, Saint Lucia, and Slovakia) and among men in 44 countries (mainly across Northern America, South America, Northern Europe, Eastern Europe, Australia, and New Zealand; Figure  2 ). The number of countries in which oropharyngeal cancer was more common than oral cavity cancer is presented in Figure  S1 . The global ASRs of oropharyngeal cancer were 0.5 per 100,000 women and 2.6 per 100,000 men (Figure  3 ). Among women, ASRs per 100,000 were highest in Denmark (2.3), France (2.0), and Czechia (2.0; Figure  4 ; see Table  S4 ); whereas Slovakia (11.1) and Romania (10.6) had the highest ASRs among men (Figure  5 ; see Table  S4 ). The lowest ASRs of oropharyngeal cancer among women were in countries in the Caribbean, Central America, and Eastern Asia and among men were in Western Africa. Nasopharyngeal cancer (C11) NPC comprised more than one half (50.8%) of the LOCP cancer incidence burden in South‐Eastern Asia (Figure  1 ). The proportions were also substantial in Northern Africa (41.8%) and Eastern Asia (36.9%), where NPC was the most frequent subsite, and in Eastern Africa (30.3%). Markedly lower proportions were observed in Melanesia‐Micronesia‐Polynesia and Northern Europe (both 2.5%). At the national level, NPC was the most common site of LOCP cancer among women in 23 countries and among men in 39 countries (mainly in Northern Africa, Middle Africa, Eastern Asia, and South‐Eastern Asia; Figure  2 ). The worldwide incidence rate of NPC was 0.7 per 100,000 in women and 1.9 per 100,000 among men (Figure  3 ; see Table  S3 ). At the national level, the highest ASRs per 100,000 women were in Brunei Darussalam (4.0), the Maldives (3.5), and Malaysia and Indonesia (both 2.8; Figure  4 ; see Table  S4 ), with rates higher in men and highest in the Maldives (10.8), Indonesia (9.6), Malaysia (8.9), and Brunei Darussalam (8.6; Figure  5 ; see Table  S4 ). Similar to the disease frequencies, elevated incidence rates were mainly seen in countries in South‐Eastern Asia and Northern Africa. Hypopharyngeal cancer (C12–C13) The contribution of hypopharyngeal cancer to LOCP cancers ranged from 1.4% in Melanesia‐Micronesia‐Polynesia to 15.8% in Eastern Europe and 15.3% in South‐Central Asia (Figure  1 ). At the national level, by sex, hypopharyngeal cancer was the most common site out of all LOCP cancers only among men in Montenegro (Figure  2B ). The global ASRs were 0.3 cases per 100,000 women and 1.6 per 100,000 men (Figure  3 ; see Table  S3 ). The highest incidence rates were seen in Bangladesh in both sexes (1.6 per 100,000 women, 9.3 per 100,000 men; Figure  3 ; see Table  S4 ). Several countries in Eastern Europe and in the Baltic regions also had rates above 5.0 per 100,000 men, namely, Hungary, Slovakia, Belarus, and Lithuania (Figure  5 ; see Table  S4 ). Salivary gland cancer (C07–C08) The contribution of salivary gland cancer to all LOCP cancers ranged from 4.0% in South‐Central Asia and 5.0% in Melanesia‐Micronesia‐Polynesia to 16.1% in Middle Africa and 21.8% in Western Africa (Figure  1 ). At the national level, salivary gland cancer was the most common site of LOCP cancer among women in 10 countries and among men in four countries (Benin, Chad, Haiti, and Togo; Figure  2 ). The ASRs of salivary gland cancer were 0.5 cases per 100,000 women and 0.7 per 100,000 men (Figure  3 ; see Table  3 ) worldwide. Countries with the highest incidence rates were Burkina Faso (1.2 per 100,000 women) and Haiti and Togo (both 1.9 per 100,000 men; Figures  4 and 5 ; see Table  4 ). Rates were relatively low among all remaining countries. Lip cancer (C00) The relative frequency of lip cancer of all LOCP cancers varied by world region and was highest in Melanesia‐Micronesia‐Polynesia (26.5%), Australia and New Zealand (20.5%), Western Asia (14.3%), Eastern Europe (14.1%), and Southern Europe (12.6%) (Figure  1 ). The lowest proportions of lip cancer were in South‐Eastern, Eastern, and South‐Central Asia (all <2.5%). At the national level, lip cancer was the most common site of LOCP cancer among women in Serbia and among men in Serbia and Turkey (Figure  2 ). The global incidence ASRs of lip cancer were 0.2 per 100,000 women and 0.5 in men (Figure  3 ; see Table  S3 ). The ASRs of lip cancer per 100,000 were highest among women in Papua New Guinea (3.3) and Australia (1.1) and among men in Papua New Guinea (8.2), Portugal (3.7), Romania (3.2), and Australia (3.2; Figures  4 and 5 ; see Table  4 ). Several countries in Eastern Europe, namely, Poland, Hungary, Serbia, and Moldova, also had comparatively higher incidence rates of lip cancer among men (>2.4 per 100,000). Countries with the lowest lip cancer ASRs for both sexes were in Eastern and South‐Eastern Asia and in the Caribbean and Central America. DISCUSSION Based on the current estimates of the global burden of LOCP cancers by subsite, cancers of the oral cavity, oropharynx, and nasopharynx were the most commonly diagnosed LOCP cancer types worldwide, although important differences between and within world regions were also evident. Incidence rates of oral cavity cancer were highest in countries across South‐Central Asia and Melanesia‐Micronesia‐Polynesia and represented the most frequently diagnosed subsite of LOCP cancers in most countries worldwide. Oropharyngeal cancer incidence rates were generally elevated in Europe and were also the most common subsite among men in North and South America as well as Australia and New Zealand. NPC was the most common subsite in countries across Northern Africa, Middle Africa, Eastern Asia, and South‐Eastern Asia, where rates were also relatively high. Below, we examine these variations in the context of subsite etiology and the prospects of effective control of the disease across the cancer continuum. Risk factors for LOCP cancers The observed incidence patterns by subsite in part reflect the prevalence and distribution of the major risk factors for LOCP cancers. For oral cavity cancer—the predominant subsite in terms of disease frequency worldwide—consumption of both smoked and smokeless forms of tobacco; areca nut, including betel quid with or without tobacco; and alcohol are the major causes and have all been classified as group 1 carcinogens by the IARC Monographs program. 4 , 20 The IARC Handbook on Oral Cancer Prevention also concluded that there is sufficient evidence that quitting consumption of these products reduces the risk of oral cancer. 21 It has been estimated that 42% of the oral cavity cancer burden globally is from tobacco smoking, 22 and drinking alcohol is estimated to contribute between 27% and 39% of oral cavity cancers in Europe and North America, respectively. 23 Although 31% of oral cavity cancer cases globally are attributable to smokeless tobacco or areca nut consumption, these products may cause up to 84% of the disease in countries associated with major consumption, including Papua New Guinea, India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, where estimated oral cancer incidence rates are also among the highest worldwide. 24 Overall, more than 95% of oral cavity cancers attributable to smokeless tobacco and areca nut are in LMICs, 24 and outcomes after an oral cancer diagnosis in these countries tend to be poorer. There is accumulating evidence over the last decades that oral HPV infection is a major cause of oropharyngeal cancer, with HPV16 and HPV18 the most high‐risk types. 5 The rising prevalence of high‐risk HPV in several higher income countries in Europe, North America, and Eastern Asia has been implicated as a major determinant of the increased incidence rates of oropharyngeal cancer—notably in men. 10 A recent global analysis reported the highest prevalence of HPV in oropharyngeal cancer in North America (73%), Oceania (62%), and Europe (45%), with HPV16 the most common subtype, accounting for 90% of all HPV‐positive cases. 6 In South America, the predominance of oropharyngeal cancer over oral cavity cancer among men may indicate a transition in the risk factor landscape in the region, with implications for prevention and policy. As incidence rates of cancers of the oral cavity decline, potentially linked to concomitant decreases in tobacco smoking, there is the prospect that HPV‐associated oropharyngeal cancer will rise in prominence among LOCP cancers globally. Whereas oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancers were the most common LOCP cancers worldwide, NPC was the most frequent form in several countries across Northern and Middle Africa as well as Eastern and South‐Eastern Asia. The etiology of NPC has viral, environmental, and genetic components. Infection with EBV is estimated to be responsible for 80% of the NPC burden in low‐incidence regions and up to 100% in high‐incidence regions. 8 In Eastern and South‐Eastern Asia, the effect of EBV might also be influenced by the presence of more virulent strains of EBV or a greater prevalence of genetic variations in the human leukocyte antigen system that encode the proteins essential for functioning of the immune system. 25 NPC incidence rates are declining in these regions, possibly as a result of reduced consumption of salt‐preserved foods containing carcinogenic N‐nitrosamines, notably in high‐risk populations within Eastern and South‐Eastern Asia and Northern Africa. 26 Reductions in tobacco smoking prevalence, a major risk factor for NPC in lower risk settings, are implicated in the declining incidence rates observed in North America and Europe. 27 Tobacco smoking is also a driver of the burden of lip and hypopharyngeal cancers that remain common in certain countries in both Oceania and Europe, although rates tend to be relatively low compared with other LOCP subsites. Exposure to UV radiation is considered as the key causal factor for cancer of the outer lip through chronic occupational or intermittent recreational exposure. 28 Incidence rates of lip cancer have either decreased or remained stable in recent decades, possibly because of reductions in the working population in outdoor occupations and increases in sun‐protective behaviors. 7 In addition to alcohol consumption, pipe smoking has been linked to cancers of the lower lip because of recurrent contact of the heated pipe stem with the lip, 29 and leaving the cigarette on the lip for an extended period while smoking has been reported to be a more important factor than the cumulative amount of tobacco smoked. 30 For hypopharyngeal cancer, alcohol consumption is also a contributing factor and carries a relative risk of 9.03 for heavy drinking (more than three drinks per day) compared with not drinking or occasional drinking, a higher risk than that observed for oropharyngeal cancer of 7.76, 31 with betel quid chewing likely playing a key role in the elevated incidence rates seen in Bangladesh. 32 Incidence rates of salivary gland cancers were relatively low across the world, but ionizing radiation, exposure to therapeutic radioactive iodine, and autoimmune disorders have been postulated as risk factors, although direct causal links have yet to be established. 33 , 34 Prevention through risk factor reduction A common theme across all LOCP cancers is their association with major preventable risk factors, i.e., tobacco, areca nut, alcohol consumption, HPV and EBV infections, and UV exposure, 4 which are also largely driven by the social and commercial determinants of health. Therefore, health promotion ensuring equitable primary prevention through policy implementation is of prime importance. To assist parties of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control to achieve its goals of implementing and managing tobacco control, the WHO introduced the MPOWER measures (Monitoring tobacco use; Protecting people from tobacco smoke; Offering help to quit tobacco use; Warning about the dangers of tobacco; Enforcing bans on tobacco advertising, promotion, and sponsorship; and Raising tobacco taxes) as critical to tobacco‐control action. Since the 2010s, a tobacco endgame strategy has emerged that seeks to accelerate tobacco control and rapidly and equitably eliminate, rather than reduce, tobacco use in the population. 35 The tobacco endgame strategy encompasses policies such as reducing the amount of nicotine in cigarettes, minimizing the number of retail outlets that sell tobacco products, and prohibiting the sale and supply of tobacco to people born after a specific year. 35 Although these strategies are generally inclusive of smokeless tobacco products, 36 global efforts on tobacco policy implementation have primarily focused on cigarettes, 37 resulting in falling global prevalence of smoking over the last 20 years. For smokeless tobacco specifically, the most common policies implemented are mandatory use of pictorial health warnings on packaging and bans on advertisements, promotions, and sponsorship. 37 Several countries have also banned the import, manufacture, and sale of specific products or of smokeless tobacco overall, as well as use in public places. 37 However, prevalence of tobacco chewing has remained stable in major consuming countries. 38 In addition, products containing areca nut without tobacco are not included under the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. Although evidence of the potential impact of tax and price increases on betel quid and areca nut initiation and use is scarce, guidelines on areca nut prevention, including banning chewing in public places, prohibiting imports and sales, increasing taxes, and putting cancer warning labels on areca nut product packaging, where appropriate, could be evaluated for inclusion in the WHO's list of the most cost‐effective policies, the so‐called best buys , in tackling noncommunicable diseases. 20 , 39 To reduce alcohol consumption in the population, the WHO's three best buys policies are increasing excise taxation, limiting purchasing availability, and reducing marketing of alcohol to the public. 40 Going beyond the three best buys , adding cancer‐specific warning labels to alcohol products, similar to those used on tobacco products, might increase awareness of the causal link with cancer and deter people from purchasing alcohol products 41 and was recommended as an action to reduce alcohol‐related cancers in the recent US Surgeon General's Advisory on Alcohol and Cancer Risk. 42 Furthermore, the Working Group of the IARC Handbook on Alcohol Control Policies concluded that interventions leading to a reduction in alcohol consumption include those that increase taxes, minimum prices, and minimum alcohol purchase or drinking age; interventions that reduce alcohol outlet density and days or hours of sale; strong alcohol marketing bans; total bans on sales; and government monopolies or other coordinated, multiple alcohol policy interventions. 43 Yet effective implementation of tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol policies relies on sustained enforcement and regulation, which are not always available or supported in countries with the most need. Prevention of HPV infection through gender‐neutral immunization programs is a key strategy to reverse the trends and reduce HPV‐associated oropharyngeal cancer burden in countries where implementation is feasible. 44 , 45 This is also an important and underestimated role for oral health professionals to educate their patients about the relation between HPV and oropharyngeal cancer and to advocate for gender‐neutral HPV vaccination to all age‐eligible patients. 46 On the role of health professionals in primary prevention, primary care practitioners should make every contact count by offering tailored prevention and cessation interventions, including brief advice using the 5A model (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange) 47 with the use of appropriate tobacco‐cessation devices, such as nicotine‐replacement therapy, alcohol‐cessation advice, and referral to specialist services where needed. 48 There is also emerging evidence on the role of dysbiosis of the oral microbiome in oral squamous cell carcinoma, 49 highlighting the importance of giving salient advice on appropriate oral hygiene as a preventive measure. Early detection of LOCP cancers Health professionals can contribute to early detection of oral cancer by conducting visual oral examinations of individuals who access their services. 50 Although it is commonly thought that this is best implemented in dental practice, it is important to decentralize early detection to health professionals across services to improve accessibility. In low‐resource settings, there is evidence that screening high‐risk populations by visual oral examination performed by trained community health care workers increases the likelihood of detecting potentially malignant disorders and oral cancers earlier and may reduce mortality from oral cavity cancer. 21 Telehealth is also emerging as a vital tool in increasing access to oral cancer early detection in rural or economically challenged areas. 51 , 52 After successful trials, population‐based screening programs are being rolled out in regions with the highest incidence of oral cavity cancer in India and China, including Taiwan. 53 , 54 However, evidence on the effectiveness of visual oral examination in reducing oral cavity cancer mortality remains limited; therefore, more robust studies are needed to assess the effectiveness of targeted screening using visual examinations and other low‐cost strategies for improving early detection and reducing mortality from oral cavity cancer. For oropharyngeal cancer, promising findings have emerged from a pilot screening trial using serology for oropharyngeal cancer in Germany, with active follow‐up of HPV‐positive patients. 55 Finally, the two overarching targets of the WHO's Global Strategy and Action Plan on Oral Health 2023–2030 56 —to ensure that oral health services are part of universal health coverage implementation and to reduce the burden of oral diseases—can accelerate prevention and improve access to early detection programs for oral cancer. Treatment and survivorship for LOCP cancers There is a substantial body of evidence‐based guidelines for the clinical management and treatment of LOCP cancers from across the world. 57 , 58 , 59 , 60 , 61 Treatment strategies for LOCP cancers vary considerably, depending on tumor location (topography) and histopathology as well as the stage at diagnosis. For squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity, surgery involving reconstruction remains the primary treatment modality. 57 However, in advanced stages—particularly in those requiring glossectomy—surgery can result in profound impairments in speech, swallowing, and overall quality of life. 62 Neoadjuvant approaches involving immunotherapy and chemotherapy are currently under investigation, and the removal of lymph nodes has been associated with improved outcomes. 62 The standard treatment regimen for oropharyngeal cancer typically involves chemoradiation with high‐dose cisplatin. Alternatively, transoral surgery may be considered when the tumor is located in an anatomically favorable and safely accessible site. 63 The prognosis of oropharyngeal cancer is partly determined by HPV status; HPV‐positive tumors are more sensitive to chemoradiation, leading to better outcomes. 63 , 64 Survival from oropharyngeal cancer has increased over time in the Nordic countries and other high‐income countries, 65 which is explained in part by the rising incidence of HPV‐positive cases. 63 In this context, de‐escalation strategies—such as reduced radiation volume and dose and reduced‐dose chemotherapy—–are being investigated to minimize long‐term treatment‐related morbidity in patients with a high likelihood of cure. 63 , 66 Because of the anatomic inaccessibility of the nasopharynx and hypopharynx, chemoradiation remains the primary treatment modality for cancers in these regions. 67 , 68 Similar to oropharyngeal carcinoma, randomized controlled trials are currently evaluating reduced‐volume radiotherapy after induction chemotherapy, with the aim of preserving survival outcomes while minimizing treatment‐related toxicities, such as acute mucositis, late‐onset otitis media, and xerostomia. 68 In contrast, most types of salivary gland cancer exhibit limited chemosensitivity and thus are managed with various combinations of surgery and radiotherapy. 33 For lip cancer, surgical excision is generally the preferred approach, offering favorable oncologic and functional outcomes with minimal long‐term aesthetic effects. 29 When detected at an early stage, most LOCP cancers are associated with favorable prognoses. However, advanced‐stage presentation remains a major contributor to poorer survival, 69 and the majority of patients are still diagnosed at an advanced stage across settings. 70 Five‐year net survival from oral cavity cancer is below 40% in India and Thailand 69 compared with >65% in the Nordic countries. 65 Similarly, survival from NPC is as high as 80% in the Nordic region 65 but around 50% or less in China and Thailand—countries where this diagnosis is more frequent. 69 Variations in availability and accessibility of cancer care services across countries significantly affect diagnosis and treatment outcomes. For example, persistent challenges in low‐resource settings, including delayed diagnosis and limited access to guideline‐recommended treatments, continue to drive outcome disparities. 71 Delayed diagnosis could be caused by lack of access to universal dental care and lower awareness of oral cancer risks or symptoms. 72 Meanwhile, advances in treatment for LOCP cancers, notably in high‐income settings, have led to improved quality of life and reduced functional and aesthetic side effects for a growing number of survivors. 73 , 74 Furthermore, social inequalities within countries, including high‐income settings, comprise a major issue that needs to be addressed to improve outcomes for all. 72 Bridging the gap both between and within countries is a major global health challenge, underscoring the need for strengthened, equitable primary prevention efforts and early detection to reduce the burden and suffering from oral cavity cancer worldwide. Strengths and limitations This study updates the global estimates of LOCP cancers by detailed subsite. Separating lip cancers from oral cavity cancers and collating cancer sites associated with HPV gives a clearer indication of the effect of primary prevention of specific risk factors on cancer burden. 1 , 11 These distinctions are often overlooked in the literature, but the variation in lip and oropharyngeal cancer rates highlights the importance of analyzing these subsites separately. However, the estimates do not distinguish between the anterior two thirds of the tongue and the oral cavity, 75 the overlapping sites of the lingual tonsil (C02.4), soft palate (C05.1), and uvula (C05.2) from the oral cavity (C02–C06), nor between HPV‐positive and HPV‐negative oropharyngeal cancers, with the latter having a worse prognosis. 10 Similarly, the group of lip cancers does not distinguish between the inner and outer or upper and lower lip, which could also have distinct etiologies, such as tobacco smoking or exposure to UV radiation. In addition, recorded incidence data from national or subnational PBCRs included in CI5 are considered of high quality because they are assessed based on their comparability, accuracy, and completeness. 16 Although the high‐quality data collected by PBCRs in 87 countries were key for conducting our study, many of these registries were subnational, and we extrapolated their data to suggest national distributions. These data were then extrapolated to the remaining 98 countries for which we did not have sufficient cancer registry data, creating additional uncertainty. This is of note particularly for some LMICs in which we estimated there to be the highest burden of oral cavity cancer, including Papua New Guinea and Bangladesh, but that do not have PBCRs. Estimates in these cases were derived from data extrapolated from neighboring countries and have demonstrated patterns similar to those in locally reported data. For example, according to cancer pathology data registered in Papua New Guinea up to 1988, although limited in population coverage, oral cavity cancer was the most common cancer among men and the second most common cancer among women. 76 Furthermore, we did not conduct a granular assessment of cancer registry completeness and data reliability by country or region, which may influence the accuracy of our incidence estimates. The coverage of high‐quality, population‐based cancer registries varies considerably across the world, with population coverage in CI5 volume XII at its highest in North America (98%), Oceania (75%), and Europe (48%) and lowest in Africa (2%) and Central and South America and the Caribbean (8%). The under‐representation of registry data from LMICs demonstrates the need for continued investment in PBCRs, which are essential surveillance systems for the robust monitoring of the local burden of cancer. This need is in contrast to persistent operational challenges faced by many registries, including limited and short‐term funding, insufficient infrastructure, and a shortage of trained personnel. 77 The IARC‐WHO Global Initiative for Cancer Registry Development ( https://gicr.iarc.who.int ) aims to address these disparities by supporting capacity building, technical assistance, and regional coordination to improve the quality, completeness, and use of cancer incidence and survival data. Although these initiatives are progressively strengthening cancer registration worldwide, the variability in data quality and coverage remains an important consideration when interpreting global incidence estimates. The national estimates we used may also serve to mask regional differences within countries. Specifically for NPC, the highest rates have been reported in PBCRs in southern regions of China, where the ASRs were up to 24.0 per 100,000 among men in the Nanhai District of Foshan City and 22.9 per 100,000 among men in Wuzhou City in 2013–2017, 16 which were significantly higher than the national average of 3.4 per 100,000 for men in China from GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates. 1 Finally, the aim of our current study was to provide an up‐to‐date estimate of the burden of LOCP cancers, and the scope did not cover trend analyses, which are addressed in other recent publications. 7 , 10 , 26 , 29 CONCLUSIONS This study provides a global snapshot of the incidence of cancers of the lip, oral cavity, and pharynx, identifying clear patterns among anatomic subsites and highlighting substantial differences between and within world regions. These variations point to distinct risk factors, emphasizing the potential for targeted policies to reduce LOCP cancer rates. Effective strategies include preventive measures—notably tobacco, alcohol, and areca nut control as well as HPV vaccination (mainly for oropharyngeal cancers)—and early detection through the visual or clinical oral screening of high‐risk populations, which should be incorporated into national cancer‐control plans. The variability in incidence across cancer subsites reinforces the importance of tailoring prevention, early detection, and treatment resources to the specific subsite profiles of each country. With the LOCP cancer incidence burden projected to increase by 60% to over 1.2 million new cases by 2050, 78 our findings reinforce the urgent need for coordinated, resource‐stratified strategies. Strengthening prevention, early detection and treatment services—tailored to the specific LOCP subsite profiles within each country—will be essential to mitigate the growing disease burden and reduce global disparities in outcomes. full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACT Cancers of the lip, oral cavity, and pharynx (LOCP) represent a substantial public health challenge worldwide. Using GLOBOCAN national estimates of incidence, detailed cancer registry data from Cancer Incidence in Five Continents , and population statistics from the United Nations, the authors report the distribution of new cases of LOCP cancers in 185 countries by sex in 2022. Age‐standardized incidence rates were calculated. For countries lacking registry data, regional averages from high‐quality registries were used to impute subsite‐specific estimates. Worldwide, 758,000 people were diagnosed with LOCP cancers in 2022, with oral cavity cancer accounting for approximately 42% of cases, followed by oropharynx (19.3%), nasopharynx (15.9%), hypopharynx (11.4%), salivary gland (7.3%), and lip (4.2%) cancers. Oral cavity cancer was the most frequent LOCP subsite among women in 141 countries and among men in 93 countries, and incidence rates were highest in countries in South‐Central Asia. Oropharyngeal cancer was the most frequent LOCP subsite among men in 44 countries and among women in five countries across Europe, Northern America, South America, Australia, and New Zealand. Nasopharyngeal cancer was the most common subsite among men in 39 countries and women in 23 countries, mainly in Northern Africa, Middle Africa, and Eastern and South‐Eastern Asia. Rates of hypopharyngeal and salivary gland cancers were low globally, although the incidence burden was greater than that of lip cancer. full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSION Based on the current estimates of the global burden of LOCP cancers by subsite, cancers of the oral cavity, oropharynx, and nasopharynx were the most commonly diagnosed LOCP cancer types worldwide, although important differences between and within world regions were also evident. Incidence rates of oral cavity cancer were highest in countries across South‐Central Asia and Melanesia‐Micronesia‐Polynesia and represented the most frequently diagnosed subsite of LOCP cancers in most countries worldwide. Oropharyngeal cancer incidence rates were generally elevated in Europe and were also the most common subsite among men in North and South America as well as Australia and New Zealand. NPC was the most common subsite in countries across Northern Africa, Middle Africa, Eastern Asia, and South‐Eastern Asia, where rates were also relatively high. Below, we examine these variations in the context of subsite etiology and the prospects of effective control of the disease across the cancer continuum. Risk factors for LOCP cancers The observed incidence patterns by subsite in part reflect the prevalence and distribution of the major risk factors for LOCP cancers. For oral cavity cancer—the predominant subsite in terms of disease frequency worldwide—consumption of both smoked and smokeless forms of tobacco; areca nut, including betel quid with or without tobacco; and alcohol are the major causes and have all been classified as group 1 carcinogens by the IARC Monographs program. 4 , 20 The IARC Handbook on Oral Cancer Prevention also concluded that there is sufficient evidence that quitting consumption of these products reduces the risk of oral cancer. 21 It has been estimated that 42% of the oral cavity cancer burden globally is from tobacco smoking, 22 and drinking alcohol is estimated to contribute between 27% and 39% of oral cavity cancers in Europe and North America, respectively. 23 Although 31% of oral cavity cancer
full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONS This study provides a global snapshot of the incidence of cancers of the lip, oral cavity, and pharynx, identifying clear patterns among anatomic subsites and highlighting substantial differences between and within world regions. These variations point to distinct risk factors, emphasizing the potential for targeted policies to reduce LOCP cancer rates. Effective strategies include preventive measures—notably tobacco, alcohol, and areca nut control as well as HPV vaccination (mainly for oropharyngeal cancers)—and early detection through the visual or clinical oral screening of high‐risk populations, which should be incorporated into national cancer‐control plans. The variability in incidence across cancer subsites reinforces the importance of tailoring prevention, early detection, and treatment resources to the specific subsite profiles of each country. With the LOCP cancer incidence burden projected to increase by 60% to over 1.2 million new cases by 2050, 78 our findings reinforce the urgent need for coordinated, resource‐stratified strategies. Strengthening prevention, early detection and treatment services—tailored to the specific LOCP subsite profiles within each country—will be essential to mitigate the growing disease burden and reduce global disparities in outcomes. addition, LOCP cancers are strongly associated with socioeconomic factors 9 and are more commonly diagnosed among men than among women and in older age groups. 3 For example, in 2022, the age‐standardized incidence rate (ASR) of LOCP cancers worldwide increased with age at diagnosis, from less than three cases per 100,000 people younger than 50 years, to 26.9 per 100,000 among people aged 50–69 years, and up to 38.0 per 100,000 cases among people aged 70 years and older. 2 Yet rates reached up to 67.4 per 100,000 among older individuals in regions with high LOCP incidence rates overall, such as Melanesia and South‐Central Asia, and 50.8 per 100,000 in Australia and New Zealand. These underlying determinants and multifactorial etiologies suggest that different factors are driving the magnitude and temporal changes in incidence rates of specific subsites and vary substantially in different populations between and within countries. For example, incidence rates of oral cavity cancer are generally decreasing among men in most world regions yet are increasing among women 7 ; meanwhile, rates of oropharyngeal cancer are steadily increasing in men and women, largely in transitioning countries. 10 This predicted growth in the burden of LOCP cancers, the complexity of the evolving patterns in incidence, and the diverse underlying etiologies make the provision of global estimates by subsite essential for health service reforms and local cancer control planning. Most prior assessments worldwide have grouped cancers together according to major disease classification groupings, obscuring the distinctive epidemiology and risk profiles of subsites. 1 , 11 Therefore, the objective of our current study was to provide a comprehensive assessment of the global burden of LOCP cancers, updating previous estimates with more recent, high‐quality cancer incidence data from population‐based cancer registries (PBCRs) by anatomic subsite. 3 For each of the LOCP cancer subsites, we assess the prospects of health promotion (through primary prevention, achieving a reduction in the underlying risk factors), early detection (mainly by visual oral examination), as well as cancer care and survivorship (including recent treatment breakthroughs) with a view to informing effective global prevention and control of LOCP cancers through the development of policies tailored to local cancer profiles. The number of cases were provided for males and females separately and by 5‐year age group according to the cancer registry. After applying these inclusion criteria, we included registry data from PBCRs in 87 countries (see Table  S1 ). We then applied the registry data proportions of cancers of the lip, base of tongue, and oral cavity to the corresponding GLOBOCAN estimates of lip and oral cavity cancer to obtain cases per subsite in 2022. At the national level, the subsite was the most frequent among women in 141 countries and among men in 93 countries, predominantly in South‐Central Asia, Southern and Western Africa, and Western Asia (Figure  2 ). The number of countries in which oral cavity cancer was more common than oropharyngeal cancer is presented in Figure  S1 . Global ASRs of oral cavity cancer were 2.0 per 100,000 women and 4.6 per 100,000 men (Figure  3 ; see Table  S3 ). The ASRs per 100,000 were highest among women in Papua New Guinea (8.1), Bangladesh (6.4), Pakistan (5.9), and India (4.7) and, among men, were highest in India (13.0), Sri Lanka (12.4), Bangladesh (12.0), Pakistan (11.3), and Papua New Guinea (9.6; Figures  4 and 5 ; see Table  S4 ). The incidence rates were also elevated among men in Southern Africa and Eastern and Southern Europe. The lowest rates were among women in countries in the Caribbean and Central America, Western Asia, and Northern and Western Africa.
